title: Pingiya's devotion (Sn 5)
hookLine: read it: the old man who can't follow the Buddha on foot but follows him in mind
tomorrow: what do old pages say when you come back to them changed?

lines: WHY DON'T YOU STAY WITH HIM?
cards: A video call with a grandparent who can't travel anymore. The screen freezes, the sound lags, and still, somehow, they're right there with you. The way to the far shore ends with a man in that spot.

Pingiya, one of the students, is old. He says so himself: weak, his eyes unclear, his hearing poor. He's gone home to his old teacher, Bavari, and someone asks him: why don't you stay with the Buddha?

teach.h: MY BODY CAN'T GO; MY MIND GOES.
teach.b: Pingiya's answer, in the closing poem of the way to the far shore, answers yesterday's question: how do you follow someone you can't reach?
My body can't go there, he says, but I go there always in thought; my mind is joined to him.

teach.h: I SEE HIM, NIGHT AND DAY.
teach.b: I see him with my mind as if with my eye, night and day, watchful, and I spend the night honoring him. So I don't think of myself as apart from him. His faith, joy, mind and mindfulness, he says, don't leave the teaching.
That's devotion, Pingiya's way: not travel, but keeping the one you follow in view. Now a neighbor who says something close.

teach.h: PSALM 16: THE LORD ALWAYS BEFORE ME.
teach.b: In the Hebrew Bible, a psalm read by Jews and Christians alike says, in the King James words: "I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved."
What they share: a person who keeps the one they follow before them, always, and finds steadiness in it. The night watch, the right hand; the same human instinct to keep someone near in mind.
And the honest difference. The psalmist sets God before him, the LORD at his right hand.
Pingiya sets before him a human teacher, honored as awakened, not as God, and his steadiness rests on his own faith and mindfulness staying with the teaching. Two ways of keeping someone close.
Neither has to become the other.

how: Buddhists recollect the Buddha (buddhanussati), bringing his qualities to mind, often before a shrine or image; Pingiya's poem is read as a picture of that practice for someone who can't be near.

o: an old student who follows his teacher in mind, not on foot
a young monk who walked to every place the Buddha had taught
a gift of flowers that a student left at the Buddha's feet

p: old and weak; can't go there
goes there always; joined to him
sees him as if with his eye
I have set the LORD always before me

s: Pingiya leaves the teaching because he's too old to travel
he says his faith, joy, mind and mindfulness don't leave it; he follows in mind.
Psalm 16 and Pingiya both picture keeping the one you follow always before you
and they differ: the psalmist sets God before him; Pingiya, a human teacher honored as awakened.
in this poem, the Buddha is worshiped as a creator God
Pingiya honors a human teacher as awakened; the poem doesn't call him God.

games.q: your old coach moved across the country, and you've got a big game Saturday. you can't call her before it. what does Pingiya's way suggest?
o: bring her to mind before the game: her voice, what she taught you.
skip thinking about her; if she isn't there, she can't help.
wait to play your best until she can come see you play.
games.why: Pingiya couldn't go on foot, so he saw his teacher with his mind as if with his eye, night and day. the teaching travels with you.

practice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable, and bring to mind someone who taught you something good: a grandparent, a coach, a teacher, a friend. See their face as clearly as you can, the way they sat or stood.
Rest with them in view, breathing slowly, until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Pingiya's devotion: an old student who can't follow the Buddha on foot, and sees him with his mind as if with his eye, night and day.

orig.note: Pali: faith, confidence; Sanskrit shraddha. Pingiya's saddha doesn't leave the teaching.

carryVoice: When distance wins the argument: I follow in mind. The way to the far shore, crossed.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 5.18 (Parayananugitigatha, the epilogue: Pingiya to Bavari); Sn 5.17 (Pingiya's question: his age and weak eyes and ears)

sources.q: I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.
